slides.page_title: The Request Pipeline & The Namespace Tree

items: DNS answers 'what IP?' — says nothing about identity
TLS answers 'right server? can anyone read this?'
Both finish before HTTP byte 1 leaves
DNS = application layer over UDP/TCP port 53
TLS sits between TCP (L4) and HTTP (L7): port 443
One name maps to many IPs — DNS spreads load
One IP serves many names — SNI picks the cert
DNS failure: NXDOMAIN, 'server not found'
TLS failure: 'connection is not private' + cert code
DNS delegates authority: root, TLD, zone
TLS chains trust: root CA, intermediate, leaf
Classic DNS and TCP carry zero encryption
DoH/DoT close the query gap; ECH hides the SNI

blocks.title: Mental Model For The Whole Book
blocks.text: DNS = phonebook: lookup plus caching. TLS = sealed envelope with a notarised ID: identity, confidentiality, integrity.
4. The Namespace Is An Inverted Tree

items: Label max 63 bytes, whole name max 255 bytes
Labels joined by dots, read right to left
FQDN ends in an implicit dot = the root zone
Levels: . then .com/.uk then example.com then api.

slides.page_title: Zones, Delegation, Server Roles & One Full Lookup

items: Zone = admin unit; domain = the whole subtree
example.com excludes eng.example.com once delegated
Delegation = parent publishes the child's NS records
Parent stores no child data, only the pointers
Glue: ns1.example.com needs its A record in the parent
13 root identities a–m.root-servers.net, not 13 machines
Anycast replicates them to 1,000+ physical instances
Transfers trigger on SOA serial bump or NOTIFY
Registry runs the TLD zone (Verisign for .com)
Registrar sells the name; registrant is you

blocks.title: Gotcha
items: Changing NS at the registrar edits the PARENT delegation
Editing records inside your zone is a different operation
Do one and forget the other = two competing truths
Root does not know www.example.com — it refers
Referral = 'ask .com', plus NS records and glue
Recursive query: client asks resolver to do the work
Iterative query: authoritative answers or refers onward
RD and RA header flags encode who recurses
Browser cache, then OS cache (systemd-resolved / dnscache)
Then /etc/hosts or the Windows hosts file
Then the configured resolver, then full recursion
hosts file wins over DNS entirely, always

blocks.title: Number-One Mystery
blocks.text: A stale hosts entry is the classic 'works on my machine but nowhere else' — check it before touching any nameserver.

items: NXDOMAIN: the name genuinely does not exist
NOERROR + empty ANSWER: name exists, no such type
Example: AAAA query against an IPv4-only host
SERVFAIL is not 'not found' — upstream timeout or DNSSEC
NOTIMP(4) = server refuses that opcode
CNAME chasing: resolver restarts at the target name
Whole chain comes back in one answer section
ndots expands 'api' to api.svc.cluster.local
That is where surprise extra lookups in Kubernetes come from
TXT carries SPF, DKIM keys, DMARC, ownership tokens
PTR: reverse under in-addr.arpa / ip6.arpa
PTR is owned by the IP block holder, not by you
SRV used by SIP, XMPP, LDAP, Minecraft
CAA restricts which CAs may issue for the domain
AAAA = 'quad-A': four times the bits of an A
Lower MX preference number wins the delivery
NS appears twice: parent delegation + child copy
SOA: primary NS, admin email (first dot = @), serial
SOA also: refresh, retry, expire, minimum = negative TTL

blocks.title: Hard Rules
items: No CNAME at the apex — apex must hold SOA and NS
Vendors fake it with ALIAS / ANAME / CNAME-flattening
CNAME cannot share a label with any other record
MX must point to a name with A/AAAA, never IP or CNAME
DNSSEC family: DNSKEY (keys), DS (hash in parent)
RRSIG (signatures), NSEC (authenticated denial)

slides.page_title: TTL Countdown, Caching & The Propagation Myth

items: Every record carries a TTL in seconds
Caches must not serve past it; it ticks down in transit
Layers: browser (~60s in Chrome), OS stub, corporate
Then ISP resolver, then public (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1)
A cache hit costs zero round trips to authoritative

blocks.title: Why The Root Survives
blocks.text: Global query volume never reaches the roots — caching absorbs it. Cache hits are the whole performance story of DNS.

items: NXDOMAIN answers are cached too (RFC 2308)
Bound is the SOA minimum field, not the record TTL
So a typo stays 'broken' for the SOA minimum
Migration: drop TTL to 60s one old-TTL period ahead
Then change, verify, then raise the TTL back
'Propagation' is a myth — nothing is ever pushed
Tail = the longest TTL still in flight somewhere
Some CPE routers ignore TTL outright
Java networkaddress.cache.ttl historically cached forever
Result: a dead IP pinned for the process lifetime
Serve-stale (RFC 8767): expired data when auth is down
Prefetch: popular records refreshed just before expiry
Port 53: UDP first for speed, TCP as fallback
AXFR zone transfer is always TCP
Message: header + Question + Answer + Authority + Additional
Header: ID, flags, four section counts
Flags: QR, AA, TC, RD, RA, 4-bit RCODE

blocks.title: TC=1 Bites
items: TC=1 means the response did not fit — retry over TCP
Firewalls blocking TCP/53 give bizarre intermittent fails
Old UDP limit 512 bytes; EDNS0 OPT advertises bigger
1232 bytes is today's common buffer, dodging fragmentation
RRSIG signs records; DS builds the chain from the root anchor
DNSSEC gives authenticity and integrity, NOT confidentiality
Validation failure shows as SERVFAIL to the client
An expired RRSIG takes a domain offline for all validators
DoH/DoT encrypt only the stub-to-resolver hop
Query history moves to the resolver operator
That is a trust transfer, not a trust elimination
Anycast: many servers share one IP, BGP picks the nearest
That is how 1.1.1.1 and the roots scale globally
Kaminsky: forged replies guarded only by a 16-bit ID
Mitigations: port randomisation, 0x20 casing, DNSSEC
Amplification: small spoofed query, huge reply — use RRL

slides.page_title: The dig Kit, Cache Flushes & Traffic Steering

items: +norecurse at the authoritative = source of truth
That is the definitive check for 'not propagating'
Windows: nslookup -type=MX example.com
Round-robin: many A records, order rotated, no health checks
GeoDNS: answer varies by resolver IP or EDNS Client Subnet
ECS is the basis of CDN latency-based steering
Failover = health checks + short TTL; TTL is the recovery floor
Split-horizon: RFC1918 inside, public addresses outside
Kubernetes CoreDNS serves svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local
Consul serves service.consul — DNS as control plane
Cache TTL there means stale endpoints, so keep it low
Wildcard *.example.com matches one undefined label only
Explicit records always beat the wildcard

blocks.title: Debug Order
items: Is it in /etc/hosts? Which resolver am I actually using?
Does the authoritative server hold the record?
Is a TTL still counting down a stale answer?
Is DNSSEC failing (SERVFAIL from validators)?
Compare parent NS set vs child NS set — lame delegation

slides.page_title: Lame Delegation Checks, TLS Guarantees & The Crypto Toolkit

lines: # sets must match, or silent outage

items: Confidentiality: nobody else reads the bytes
Integrity: nobody alters them undetected
Authentication: you reached the right server
NOT provided: availability, authorization, endpoint safety
Also not hidden: traffic size and timing
SSL 2.0/3.0 broken and disabled everywhere
TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated in 2021; 1.2 and 1.3 are current
'SSL certificate' is a legacy misnomer for an X.509 cert
Core trick: asymmetric once to agree a symmetric key
Then symmetric crypto for all bulk data
TLS 1.3 permits AEAD only — kills MAC-then-encrypt bugs
Diffie-Hellman derives a shared secret over a public channel
ECDHE = ephemeral elliptic-curve variant (X25519, P-256)

blocks.title: Forward Secrecy
blocks.text: ECDHE keys are discarded after use, so stealing the long-term private key later cannot decrypt yesterday's recorded traffic. Static RSA had no such property.

items: Cert key proves identity by signing handshake data
It does not encrypt the session key in modern TLS
1.3 ships five suites total instead of hundreds
Record layer: chunks up to 16KB, AEAD-protected payload

slides.page_title: The TLS 1.2 Handshake, Message By Message

items: ClientHello: client random, versions, suite list, extensions
Extensions carry SNI, ALPN, curves, signature algorithms
ServerHello: server random, one chosen suite, version, session ID
Certificate: leaf plus intermediates, chain order matters
Root is optional and normally omitted from the chain
ServerKeyExchange: ephemeral DH public key, signed by cert key
That signature is what proves ownership of the certificate
ServerHelloDone, then ClientKeyExchange with client key share
Both sides compute the pre-master secret via ECDHE
Mix with both randoms through the PRF: master secret
Derive four keys: client/server encryption + MAC
ChangeCipherSpec, then Finished on each side
Finished hashes the whole transcript — tampering breaks it

blocks.title: The Cost
blocks.text: Two full round trips before a single byte of application data. That price is exactly why TLS 1.3 was designed.

items: Static RSA: client encrypts pre-master with server public key
Simple, no forward secrecy, removed in TLS 1.3
mTLS: server sends CertificateRequest for a client cert
Client replies Certificate + CertificateVerify over transcript
Used for service-to-service auth and zero-trust networks

caption.text: Four round trips happen before your browser sends a single byte of HTTP — and most outages live in those four. This handbook walks the whole path: DNS hierarchy, delegation, glue, TTL maths and the propagation myth, then TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 handshakes, X.509 chains, cleartext SNI and ECH. Ends with the mistakes that break both and the exact dig and openssl commands that find them.
